name: Start Here
subtitle: Twelve records, chronological, nothing difficult
blurb: One easy record from each stage of the music, in order. Nothing here is demanding; the point is to hear the ground shifting between 1921 and today without anyone shouting at you.

steps.bridge: Begin with one man and a piano, because that is where the machinery is most visible: a marching left hand and a right hand refusing to land with it.
Johnson had to be his own band; Armstrong had one, and then discovered he did not need it either — this is where the soloist takes over jazz.
Armstrong showed that a singer could phrase like a horn; Holiday shows what happens when someone takes that permission and uses it on the words.
Same decade, opposite scale: instead of five players listening to each other, fifteen executing a composer's design, with the improvising rationed.
The big bands have collapsed and the small group is back, but now it plays too fast to dance to and the harmony moves twice as often.
Bebop had become a specialist's music; this is the correction — the same harmony slowed down with the blues and the church put back into it.
Hard bop gives a soloist a chord every two beats. Here Miles Davis takes almost all of them away and finds out what is left to play.
Coltrane was on the previous record. Five years later he takes the same reduced harmony and aims it at something other than music.
Davis again, and the instruments have changed: electric piano, electric guitar, and eighth notes that no longer swing.
Hancock played electric piano on that record. Four years later he builds a band where the groove is the composition and the solo is a passenger.
A generation decides electricity was a wrong turn, goes back to acoustic instruments, and plays them with conservatory precision and considerable force.
And a generation after that decides the argument was never worth having, and builds jazz out of Afrobeat, dub and grime instead.

name: The Full Arc
subtitle: Thirty records, ragtime to now
blurb: The historical spine in order. Some of it is hard going and that is deliberate — this is the route that shows you how each thing came out of the last one, including the parts that came out of an argument.

steps.bridge: Before jazz: composed piano music with the syncopation written in, no improvising, no blues. Everything downstream inherits the rhythmic habit and discards the rest.
The first jazz record, made by a white New Orleans band who then claimed to have invented the music. Hold both of those facts at once.
In Harlem, ragtime's left hand gets loosened and swung and turned into a competitive sport at rent parties.
Back to New Orleans, properly this time: three horns improvising simultaneously, and a second cornet player who will not stay in the background much longer.
That second cornet player. Across three years the collective front line stops being the point and the soloist becomes it.
The first evidence that this music could be rebuilt somewhere else: Paris, no drums, no horns, and a guitar language from Romani string tradition.
Meanwhile in New York, a singer and a tenor player work out how to have a conversation across a mediocre pop song.
Kansas City arrives and changes the floor everyone is standing on — an even four, timekeeping moved to the cymbals, and enormous space.
The peak of the written tradition, by a composer who wrote for specific people rather than for parts, which is why nobody else can play it properly.
And the reaction: the big band abandoned, the dance floor abandoned, the tempo doubled, and the harmony made deliberately harder to follow.
Four years later the same harmony is played at half the temperature, with written counterpoint and a French horn, by people including a very young Miles Davis.
A different reaction to bebop entirely: keep the harmony and the soloing, replace the swing feel with clave, and the whole rhythmic basis changes.
Back in New York the correction to cool jazz is heat — gospel chords, a backbeat, and tunes you can actually hum.
In Rio, musicians listening to the cool jazz records take the restraint, add samba and much harder harmony, and invent something Brazil still argues about.
Davis's answer to hard bop's congestion: take away nearly all the chords and see what a soloist does with the silence.
The same year, in a different city, someone takes away the chords entirely and keeps the tune. The reception was hostile and personal.
None of that argument reached the neighbourhood bars, where the Hammond organ was doing perfectly well and the audience answered out loud.
Musicians who heard Ornette Coleman and went partway: forms that will not resolve, harmony that will not declare a key, and a rhythm section that argues back.
Coltrane in the same year, using the reduced harmony for something else — a suite structured as a religious offering, with a chant where the head should be.
Chicago's answer to New York's free jazz: a musicians' collective, composed sections, small instruments, and long stretches where almost nothing happens.
Davis's second quintet holding a pulse while treating the harmony as negotiable — the last acoustic thing he did before plugging in.
By now the music has left the country for good: Tokyo takes the modal template and plays it harder, recorded better than almost anything in America.
Davis plugs in, hires thirteen people, and lets a producer assemble the record out of tape splices afterwards. The argument this started lasted twenty years.
One of those thirteen forms a band where the groove is the composition, sells enormously, and gets called a sell-out for it.
In Europe an entirely different reaction to the same decade: one man, one out-of-tune piano, no plan, and no volume at all.
And in New York the avant-garde, priced out of every club, rents lofts and puts on its own concerts. This is what a weeknight sounded like.
The counter-revolution: acoustic instruments, formidable technique, and a public argument that the previous fifteen years had been a mistake.
While that argument runs, producers in the same city are lifting two-bar loops off the jazz records nobody was buying and building something else out of them.
Twenty years on, musicians raised on both sides of that split make a three-hour spiritual jazz record with a choir and put it out on an electronic label.
And in London, a scene that came up through a free youth programme plays jazz for people who are standing up, on rhythms from Lagos, Kingston and Port of Spain.

name: Into the Deep End
subtitle: Fifteen records that get progressively harder
blurb: Free, spiritual and avant-garde music, sequenced so each record teaches your ear what it needs for the next one. Do not start at the bottom of this list. It will not go well.

steps.bridge: Start with a song you already know, stretched to thirteen minutes over two chords. Nothing here is strange yet; you are just learning to wait.
Now the avant-garde with a bass line and a backbeat, so you can hear that free playing and a groove are not opposites.
Keep the singable melody and the steady pulse, and remove one thing only: the chord sequence. That single subtraction is what all of this is built on.
Same reduction, aimed at devotion rather than at freedom — a four-note figure and a mantra holding forty minutes together.
Now remove the chord changes entirely and replace them with a drone, and add a harp. Your ear stops looking for movement and starts listening to colour.
A gentle pentatonic melody that goes somewhere violent and comes back. This is your first taste of an ecstatic build, with a safe route home.
Back to a composed record, but everything wobbles — no piano stating the harmony, and a drummer playing around the beat rather than on it.
Two quartets improvising at once, one in each speaker. Follow one at a time until you can hear both, then decide what you think about it.
Now the melodies get simpler and the playing gets more extreme. It is a hymn and a howl, and the tune always survives.
Eleven players alternating between collective density and single solos. If you can hear that alternation, the wall becomes a structure.
A completely different route to freedom: atonal, percussive and organised by written units rather than by feel. Nothing about this comes from the blues.
Chicago's opposite proposition — silence and space as the material, and a refusal to keep blowing simply because the tape is running.
Europe rejecting all of the above, including the blues and the pulse, at maximum volume for the entire record. There is a written theme; find it.
One saxophone, no breathing pauses, producing several simultaneous lines. By now you should be listening to texture rather than for melody.
Finish where there is nothing left to hold: tenor and drums, no bass, no harmony, no meter. Recorded five months before he died.
